708.title: The penance grove
708.hook: he visits ascetics who hope for heaven through pain, and moves on (Buddhacarita 7)
708.howItsDone: Buddhist teaching often describes the Buddha's path as a middle way between indulgence and harsh self-punishment, and monastic rules in some communities include not eating after midday and simple living, but not self-torment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chandaka, thanked and sent home with the jewels. Your line: sent home with the jewels. A new week begins inside the forest.

Some of them eat only grass and leaves, the poem says, grazing like deer. Some live on what falls from the trees. Some stand in water. Some tend sacred fires and offer into them day and night. This is the hermitage the prince walks into, his hair freshly cut, his silk traded for a plain robe. The people here have given up far more than jewels, and they come out to greet him with wonder. If anyone could teach him, it ought to be them. So he asks.
screen: `GRASS, LEAVES, WATER, FIRE.` → `THEY GREET HIM WITH WONDER.` → `SO HE ASKS.`

segments.voice: First, the question. The prince asks one of the elders plainly what all this is for: the hunger, the cold water, the hard ways of living. Second, the answer. These hardships are a kind of payment. Suffer now, and win heaven after death, or a happier life to come. Pain in this life buys pleasure in the next. Third, the prince's reply, given here in paraphrase. He honors their effort, but turns the logic over and finds a problem. If you suffer now to enjoy later, you're still chasing enjoyment; you've only moved it further off. And heaven, as they describe it, ends too, the way all merit runs out, and then the round of birth begins again. He's looking for a way out of the round, not a better seat on it. And a second problem: it's the mind that drives a person toward harm or good. Torment the body and leave the mind untamed, and you've punished the servant for what the master did. Fourth, the leaving. He stays a few nights, watching and asking, then decides to go. The ascetics are sorry to lose him and ask him to stay. One of them points him toward a teacher further on, a sage named Arada, whom the poem will reach later. The prince thanks them, and goes. He doesn't call these people fools. He calls their aim too small. They were brave and sincere, paying with pain for something that wouldn't last. He keeps the bravery and drops the bargain.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one hard thing you do on purpose, an alarm before dawn, a strict diet, staying late every night, saying yes when you're already tired, and ask the prince's question quietly: what am I hoping this pain will buy? Some hardships buy something real and good; some are bargains that never pay out. You don't have to decide which this is; just look at it honestly, then come back to the breath.
The penance grove. A forest hermitage where ascetics endure hardship hoping for heaven; the prince honors their effort, finds their aim too small, and moves on. Today's word.
Your line: not through pain. Whatever he's looking for, it can't be bought that way. Day seven hundred eight, done.

709.title: The palace mourns
709.hook: Yasodhara's lament: why did he leave without me? (Buddhacarita 8)
709.howItsDone: Yashodhara is remembered in Buddhist tradition, and in later tellings she becomes a nun herself; her lament is part of how some Buddhists reflect on the cost of the prince's leaving to those who loved him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the penance grove, where pain was a payment for heaven. Your line: not through pain.

An empty saddle. That's what the city sees first. Kanthaka comes back through the gate with no rider, and Chandaka walks beside him holding a bundle of jewels. People run into the streets, looking past the horse for the prince, and he isn't there. The horse has come home. The rider hasn't. For a whole canto now, the poem leaves the hero in the forest and stays behind with everyone he left.
screen: `AN EMPTY SADDLE.` → `THE CITY RUNS OUT.` → `THE POEM STAYS BEHIND.`

segments.voice: First, the city. The poem fills the streets with weeping. Not long ago people watched the prince ride out in splendor. Now the city feels like a house after a funeral. Second, the women of the palace, and Gautami, the queen who raised him after his mother died. She grieves over small, precise things, the way people do: his long, beautiful hair, now cut and lying somewhere on the forest floor. Third, Yashodhara, his wife. Her grief comes out as anger first, at Chandaka and even at the horse: why did you take him? Then it turns to the question underneath. In paraphrase, she asks why he left without her. If he wanted the holy life, why not with her? She remembers the kings of old, his own ancestors in the stories, who went into the forest with their wives beside them. He has gone to seek the highest good, she says, and left his partner behind, as if the good were something to be won alone. She isn't asking him to stay a prince. She's asking why she had no part in the leaving. And fourth, the king. When Shuddhodana hears, the poem says, he falls to the ground in grief. All his walls, all his music, and the son is gone anyway. A story like this could skip this part. Ashvaghosha keeps the camera in the palace and lets the grief speak in full, without arguing with Yashodhara or hurrying her. The leaving was right for the prince, the poem believes, and it still cost someone.

710.title: The ministers' arguments
710.hook: the king's ministers come to bring him home, with every argument they have (Buddhacarita 9)
710.howItsDone: Buddhist communities teach the prince's resolve in this scene as an example of determination, and in some communities the story of family members asking a renunciant to come home is part of how people talk about ordination and the families of monks and nuns.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yashodhara, and a palace in mourning. Your line: the one left behind.

Your father is burning with grief. That's the opening line of the case, more or less, and it's delivered by two men who have walked a long way to say it. The king can't go himself, so he sends his family priest and his minister, with one job: bring the prince home. They find him resting under a tree. They bow. And then they begin, and they've come prepared.
screen: `TWO MEN FROM THE PALACE.` → `ONE JOB: BRING HIM HOME.` → `THEY'VE COME PREPARED.`

segments.voice: First, the heart. The priest speaks for the family: your father's grief, the queen who raised you, your wife, your small son. Come back for them. Second, the head. You can practice what is right at home, as a king. Kings of old found freedom while they still ruled. There will be time for the forest later, when you're old and the throne has passed on. Third, the doubt. The minister tries a different road. Who really knows what comes after death? Some teachers say there's another life, some say there isn't. Some say things simply happen by their own nature, the way a thorn is sharp without anyone sharpening it. Why give up everything for a question no one can settle? Love, duty, tradition, and doubt itself: they use every argument they have. Fourth, the answer. The prince hears each man out and answers each in turn. In paraphrase, he tells the priest he knows his father's love, and it grieves him, but parting will come anyway, by death if not by this. To the minister he says he won't take this question secondhand, from whichever teacher sounds surest. He'll find out for himself. He would sooner walk into fire than go home with his search unfinished. He stands and walks on, and the two men go home slowly, the poem says, looking back. Udayin argued from pleasure. These two argue from love, and then from doubt. And to doubt, the prince doesn't answer with a certainty of his own. He answers with a search.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a time someone pushed you hard to change your mind, and notice where the pressure shows up in your body, the jaw, the shoulders, the chest; breathe into that place. Then picture yourself the way the prince sits under the tree, hearing each point, not raising your voice, not folding. Let your feet press into the floor, and feel how steady the ground stays under all that talk.

711.title: Bimbisara's visit
711.hook: the king offers half his kingdom (Buddhacarita 10)
711.howItsDone: Bimbisara appears in other Buddhist stories as a king friendly to the Buddha, and the meeting on the hill outside Rajagriha is told in the Pali discourses as well as in this poem.

segments.voice: Yesterday: doubt, and the prince's answer to it, a search. Your line: every argument.

A city ringed by hills, and a young man in a plain robe walking its streets with a bowl. The poem says people stop what they're doing to look at him. Those walking stand still. Those standing follow. People at windows lean out. He doesn't look like a beggar, whatever he's carrying. In a palace above the streets, another king is watching too. He doesn't know who this is. But he wants to.
screen: `A CITY RINGED BY HILLS.` → `THE WHOLE STREET STOPS.` → `A KING IS WATCHING.`

segments.voice: First, the city. The prince has crossed the Ganges and come to Rajagriha, the royal city of Magadha. He goes for alms, eats what he's given, and climbs a hill outside the town to rest. Second, the king. Bimbisara, king of Magadha, sees him from his palace and sends someone to follow him and find where he stays. Then he goes himself, up the hill with only a few attendants, and sits down with the young wanderer as an equal. Third, the offer. Bimbisara speaks as a friend. In paraphrase: I know your family, a great royal line. You're young and strong, and you've left a throne to beg. This doesn't suit you. Take half of my kingdom. Rule beside me. Then he lays out a sensible plan for a life: youth for pleasure, the middle years for wealth, old age for religion. Do things in their season. Fourth, the spirit of it. This isn't a trap, and it isn't a bribe. The poem presents Bimbisara as generous and sincere: he looks at a stranger and sees someone worth half of everything he has, and helps the only way a king knows how. That's what makes this harder than yesterday. The ministers came to take the prince back. Bimbisara comes to give him more. The prince listens, and doesn't reach for the offer. His reasons fill the whole next canto. Today, the offer just hangs in the air, held out with an open hand.

712.title: Passions spurned
712.hook: the prince explains why pleasures don't satisfy: fire isn't quenched by fuel (Buddhacarita 11)
712.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use fire as a picture of craving, and in the Pali discourses the Buddha's Fire Sermon describes the senses as burning; in some Buddhist meditation practices people watch a craving rise and fall without acting on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bimbisara's visit, and a generous offer of half a kingdom. Your line: half a kingdom.

Throw a log on a fire and ask it whether it's had enough. It hasn't. It's bigger now, and hungrier. That's the picture at the center of the prince's answer to King Bimbisara, who has just offered him half a kingdom and a sensible plan for enjoying life in its season. The prince doesn't brush the king off. He takes the offer seriously enough to give a whole canto of reasons, and the fire is where he begins.
screen: `A LOG ON THE FIRE.` → `BIGGER, AND HUNGRIER.` → `A WHOLE CANTO OF REASONS.`

segments.voice: First, the respect. Before any argument, the prince honors the king's kindness: it's no surprise, he says in paraphrase, that a man of good family would offer friendship like this, and he's grateful. Second, the fire. Pleasures don't satisfy. A fire isn't quenched by fuel, and the sea isn't filled by the rivers that run into it. Feed a desire and you don't end it; you make it larger. Someone who gets what they wanted wants more; someone who gets more fears losing it. Third, the pictures. The poem piles them up. Pleasures are like a dog gnawing a dry bone, never fed by it. Like a scrap of meat that birds fight over. Like a torch of straw carried into the wind, which burns the hand that holds it. Like a dream that's gone when you wake. Like borrowed jewelry that has to be given back. Each says the same thing from a different side: what we reach for to soothe the burning keeps the burning going. Fourth, the parting. He tells the king he isn't running from enemies or from hardship. He's going after freedom, and he can't be turned aside by a kingdom any more than by threats. And the poem ends gently. Bimbisara joins his palms, wishes him success, and asks one favor: when you've found what you're seeking, come back and show it to me. The prince promises. He turns down the passions, not the king. He refuses half a kingdom and keeps a friend.

713.title: The teacher Arada
713.hook: he learns the deep states and finds them not final (Buddhacarita 12)
713.howItsDone: The deep meditative states the prince learned from his first teachers are still described in Buddhist meditation teaching, where they are counted as refined states of mind, valued but not the same as awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday: passions spurned, half a kingdom refused and a friend kept. Your line: fuel doesn't quench fire.

What does it feel like to master the hardest thing your teacher knows, and then ask, is that all? The prince is about to find out. Back in the penance grove, someone pointed him toward a sage named Arada. Now he's sitting in front of him. Arada is everything the grove wasn't: calm, learned, a teacher of deep meditation, not of pain. He welcomes the young wanderer warmly. And he begins to teach.
screen: `MASTER IT, THEN ASK: IS THAT ALL?` → `ARADA WELCOMES HIM.` → `THE TEACHING BEGINS.`

segments.voice: First, the map. Arada explains the world as he sees it: a nature that changes and unfolds, and a knower who watches it. Suffering comes from not telling the two apart. Free the knower from what it watches, and you're free. Second, the ladder. Leave home. Live simply. Settle the mind. Then rise through deeper and deeper states of meditation, leaving more behind at each step, until the mind rests in a state of nothingness, where nothing at all is held. That, Arada says, is liberation. Third, the prince learns it, and practices. The old Pali discourses tell this part too, where the teacher is called Alara Kalama: the Buddha later says he reached that same state of nothingness under him, and that Arada offered to lead the community with him, as an equal. The student had matched the master. Fourth, the question. Here the poem gives the prince his doubt, in paraphrase: if the knower is still there at the top of the ladder, then something is still there that can be bound again, like a seed that's been kept dry. Give it rain, and it sprouts. Nothingness is deep, and quiet, and good, but it isn't the end of the road. So he thanks Arada and leaves. The poem has him try one more teacher, Udraka, who teaches a state subtler still, and he finds the same thing there. He learns all they have to give, reaches the top of it, and then, honestly, keeps going.

segments.voice: Follow ten breaths, counting each one all the way to ten, and if you lose count, start again. When you reach ten, notice the small satisfaction of finishing. Then ask gently, without any pressure, is there more here, and keep breathing without counting to see what's left when the task is done.

714.title: Nandabala's milk
714.hook: after the fasting, a herdsman's daughter gives him milk-rice (Buddhacarita 12)
714.howItsDone: The offering of milk-rice is remembered in Buddhist art and festivals, and giving food to monks and nuns is a daily practice in some Buddhist communities, where the gift is received as part of the path.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nothingness, a deep state the prince mastered and found not final. Your line: not final.

A bowl of rice cooked in milk. Plain food, the kind a grandmother makes for someone who's been sick. In this canto it changes the story. The prince has left his teachers and gone to live by a river, and now, with no one left to learn from, he tries the one road he hasn't tried: fasting, as hard as a body can bear. In the penance grove he told the ascetics that pain wasn't the way. Now he tests it on himself.
screen: `A BOWL OF MILK-RICE.` → `NO TEACHERS LEFT.` → `HE TESTS THE HARD ROAD HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: First, the fasting. On the bank of the river Nairanjana, the poem says, he cuts his food down and down, until he lives on almost nothing. His body wastes away. Some companions, also seeking freedom, settle near him, admiring his discipline and waiting for him to break through. Second, the turn. He doesn't break through. He breaks down. And he sees why, in paraphrase: this isn't the way to freedom. A mind can't settle when the body is starving. Calm needs some strength under it. Third, the milk. He bathes in the river, weak, and comes up out of the water slowly. Then comes Nandabala, the daughter of a chief of the herdsmen, moved by the gods, the poem says, to come to him. She bows and offers him a bowl of milk-rice. He takes it. He eats. And strength returns. Fourth, the cost. His companions watch him eat, decide he has given up, and leave him. The poem doesn't defend him; it lets the moment be. A woman with a bowl did what no teacher and no hardship could: she gave him back his body, so his mind could do its work. Other tellings give her a different name, Sujata, and other details; this poem calls her Nandabala. Look back over the week: a grove that sought heaven through pain, a palace in grief, ministers with every argument, a king with half a kingdom, fire that fuel can't quench, a teacher whose best was not final, and now a bowl of milk-rice, taken with thanks.
screen: `FASTING BY THE RIVER.` · `A STARVED BODY, AN UNSETTLED MIND.` · `NANDABALA'S BOWL.` · `HIS COMPANIONS WALK AWAY.` · then, large: `STRENGTH RETURNS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place where you've been going it alone, harder than you need to, and one person who has offered help, or would if you asked. Picture them holding out a bowl, notice what in you wants to wave it away, and then picture taking it with both hands and saying thank you. Feel what changes in your body when you're not carrying it alone.
Nandabala's milk. After fasting brings him no closer, a herdsman's daughter offers the prince milk-rice; he eats, his strength returns, and his companions leave him. Today's word.
Your line: strength returns. What's left now is a tree, and the night. Day seven hundred fourteen, done.
